newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Zinc miners aim for lower treatment charges.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Zinc miners aim for lower treatment charges.

text.p: Australian zinc miners said on Monday they were set to begin their annual ritual of negotiating next year's treatment and refining charges with independent smelters in the expectation of improving on 1996 terms.

The miners will argue that while it is unlikely there will be less concentrates headed for smelters next year, production curtailments, mainly in the arctic region, will nonetheless create more of a market for their intermediate material.

"You can go right around the world and I think you'd find that most mines have not produced up to expectations and in fact have produced a lot less," a negotiator close to the Asian zinc markets said.
Also, China is seen lapping up more of the West's concentrate supplies as its capabilities to smelt zinc outrun the domestic concentrate pool.
"(China will) provide an outlet for what would otherwise be an untenable surplus of concentrate in the West," brokerage JB Were & Son argues in its latest commodities report.
The negotiations will begin in earnest following the October 10 meeting of the International Lead and Zinc Study Group, where the focus will be on supply and demand tallies and forecasts.

Both sides say they will seek to use data from the group as bargaining chips during the typically lengthy negotiating process, saying it would be surprising if next year's terms were cemented much before the American Zinc Association meeting in February.

The long-suffering smelters of Europe, where over-capacity and weak demand are causing losses, are expected to resist any early agreements in the hopes a hard-line stance will pay off with more favourable terms.
"The Europeans are not making money and they will be very very tough," said an Australian metals trader.
Zinc treatment charges in 1996 were fixed at US$190.00 a tonne, basis a London Metal Exchange price of $1,000 a tonne, representing a $15.00 leap from 1995 in favour of the smelters.
"This year they (miners) will seek an improvement and they will probably get one," said a metals trader.
"I'd be looking for perhaps a $5.00 improvement on last year, taking the charge to about $185.00 a tonne," he said.
An industry view last year that the market for concentrates would fall deeper into surplus failed to develop, leaving miners with more clout at the negotiating table, he said.
Traders point to a relatively tight spot market for zinc, where terms are averaging about $170.00 a tonne.
"Demand is strong, but there is little if any surplus concentrates to sell," one said.
"We'd be pretty disappointed if they stayed flat," a negotiator for a large international mining house told Reuters.
"While there's probably going to be a little bit more around, there are some problems at the mine end," he said.

Miners also hope to point to improving market conditions for zinc metal, which if accompanied by a rise in price would allow smelters to better their margins. "Demand for the product is increasing, albeit slowly, and consumption is still exceeding production," a negotiator for one of the miners said.
Longer term, a rise in treatment charges to $200.00 a tonne will be acheived by the smelters by 2000, Australia's AME Mineral Economics Ltd forecasts.
But AME says such price gains would so pinch higher cost miners that concentrate output would have to be reduced.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
